analysis.title: Taiwan's rising income terms of trade
key_insights: Taiwan's nominal GDP rose 19% y/y in H1 2026 and 20.0% on a four-quarter rolling basis, supported by rising income terms of trade.
Real GDP grew 14.1% y/y in H1 2026, the strongest H1 in decades. Q1 was revised to 15.4% y/y and Q2 was 12.9% y/y.
Merchandise exports rose 61% y/y in Q3. ANZ expects resilient semiconductor exports and AI-related capex to keep supporting double-digit GDP growth in H2.

Taiwan has benefited more than South Korea from the AI upcycle. Semiconductors are 35% of Taiwan's exports versus 36% for South Korea, but Taiwan's export-to-GDP ratio was 85% in Q2 versus 50% for South Korea, whose economy is more diversified.

ANZ's simple regression finds that changes in income terms of trade explain around 62% of Taiwan's nominal GDP growth over the last two decades. The link has strengthened in recent years because of Taiwan's position in high-performance chips.
Taiwan's net terms of trade fell 4.6% in Q3 2026 because import prices rose faster than export prices over the last two quarters, driven by higher energy prices.

Rising semiconductor prices partly offset higher import costs. ANZ calls this 'chipflation' and says it is unprecedented in the series since the early 2000s, which sets the current AI boom apart from earlier tech cycles.

Key risk 1: Taiwan's exposure to the AI investment cycle. ANZ does not say the boom is ending, but cites concerns over the scale and financing of AI capex. If the SOX index remains a reliable leading indicator, the outlook for Taiwan's exports could become more uncertain.

Key risk 2: energy costs. Taiwan imports most of its energy and chip manufacturing is power intensive. The Q2 and Q3 decline in net terms of trade is read as an early warning that energy import costs may eventually outpace the gains from chip pricing.

sector_views.rationale: Chip prices and volumes are lifting Taiwan's export income, but the cycle is exposed to AI capex overbuilding and rising energy costs.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Supported by rising income terms of trade from chip volume and price gains.

macro_indicators.indicator: Taiwan nominal GDP growth, four-quarter rolling
macro_indicators.interpretation: Shows the nominal boom is sustained, not a one-quarter spike.
Revised figure, part of the H1 outperformance.
Growth remained exceptionally strong, though slower than Q1.
Reflects AI-related semiconductor demand in both volume and price.
Import prices, led by energy, rose faster than export prices. ANZ treats it as an early warning signal.
ANZ expects semiconductor exports and AI capex to support double-digit growth.

risk_factors: Overbuilding of digital infrastructure globally could hit Taiwan's chip-heavy export growth.
Concerns over the scale and financing structure of AI capex.
Higher imported energy costs could raise inflation, increase production costs and squeeze chip-sector profitability.
Falling net terms of trade in Q2 and Q3 may signal that energy import costs will outpace chip pricing gains.
charts_described: Figure 1 compares Taiwan's nominal GDP growth with Asian peers, with Taiwan standing out.
Figure 2 shows Taiwan's nominal growth and income terms of trade strongly correlated, with the regression explaining around 62% of nominal GDP growth over two decades.
vol_and_positioning: ANZ says the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) may serve as a leading indicator for Taiwan's exports. The report compares the SOX 2026-2027 path with 1999-2000 (Figure 5).

tension_points.bull_case: Chip volume and price gains lift income terms of trade, and ANZ expects double-digit GDP growth in H2 on resilient semiconductor exports and AI capex.
tension_points.bear_case: Overbuilding of AI infrastructure and rising energy costs could reverse the gains. Net terms of trade already fell 4.6% in Q3, and the SOX index may signal weaker exports.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A weaker SOX index as a leading signal for exports, or energy import costs outpacing chip price gains.

theme_stances.key_argument: Chip pricing and export volumes are lifting Taiwan's income terms of trade and nominal GDP, partly offsetting higher energy import costs.
theme_stances.evidence: Unprecedented chip price gains stemming from the AI boom have partly offset higher energy costs

theme_stances.evidence: high concentration in chips is a double-edged sword
